# v1 Scope Decision: Recommended Cut Line, Risks, and Release Gates

**Emma Clarke, Product Lead — AtlasFlow Beta**
*Sources: Product Brief, Architecture Note, Risk Register, Ticket Spec, QA Matrix, UX Copy*

---

## The Answer First

**Ship comments-only collaboration. Not full collaboration. Not a delayed reliability-first hold.**

This is not a compromise position. It is the correct scope given what users actually need, what the architecture can safely support, and what the team can ship with integrity in four weeks.

---

## The Recommended Cut Line

### IN — v1 Beta Ships This

| Feature | Rationale |
|---|---|
| **Comments on specs** (append-only, flat, entity-level) | 3 engineering days, no data model concurrency risk, directly closes the "decisions lost in Slack" pain loop |
| **Review requests** (open → addressed → closed) | 2 days, maps to real user workflow, directly drives the week-one activation metric |
| **Decision history** (visible record linked to comment/review thread) | The leading retention signal — users who create a decision record in week one return in week two at a meaningfully higher rate |
| **Activity feed** (explicit actions only: comment created, review requested, decision recorded) | 1 day, covers audit trail without leaking passive presence or read behavior |
| **Workspace-level roles: owner / editor / viewer** | Already modelled; enforcement gates all of the above safely |

**Total estimate: 6–8 engineering days.** Bounded. Testable. Shippable with confidence.

### OUT — Not v1

| Feature | Why it's out |
|---|---|
| **Live co-editing** | Requires CRDT/OT strategy, conflict resolution, undo/redo semantics, object-level permissions, editor reconciliation. 4–6 weeks minimum done responsibly. This is an architectural commitment, not a feature addition. Hard out. |
| **Live presence / cursors** | Looks cosmetic; is not. Introduces heartbeat timing, stale session cleanup, privacy exposure, and implied real-time guarantees the system cannot back up. Presence that lies is worse than no presence. |
| **Object-level permissions** | Not available in v1 architecture. All current permissions are workspace-level. Building this now contaminates the data model before we have usage signal on what the right permission shape even is. |
| **Private comment threads** | Requires object-level visibility controls. Blocked by the above. |
| **Guest / external access** | Hard block — pending object-level permission model per Risk Register. |
| **Email / Slack notifications** | Out of ticket scope. Do not let notification infrastructure scope-creep into beta. |
| **Full RBAC** | Ships as internal plumbing only. Enforcement deferred to v1.1 against a reviewed data model. |

---

## Risks We Accept

These are known, documented, and survivable. Accepting them is a deliberate product call, not an oversight.

**1. Resolve/unresolve race condition (last-write-wins)**
Two users resolving the same comment nearly simultaneously will resolve to the last write. This is acceptable for v1 *if and only if* the event history shows actor and timestamp so the outcome is legible. Not a trust bug. A minor UX edge case.
*Source: Risk Register, Risk 5*

**2. Comments appear contextually displaced after spec edits**
A comment made on version N of a spec may look slightly out of context after the spec is updated. Mitigation: store spec version ID on every comment and surface a "made on previous version" label where relevant. Users will encounter this; it should not surprise them.
*Source: Risk Register, Risk 3 / Ticket Spec acceptance criteria*

**3. Mention notification is a stub**
Mentioning a teammate in v1 does not trigger email or Slack notification. Users who expect notification will not get it. This must be set as an explicit expectation in onboarding copy — not discovered by accident.
*Source: Ticket Spec, out of scope list*

**4. Decision history depends on user behavior, not automation**
Decision records are created explicitly. If teams don't form the habit, the retention signal doesn't fire. This is a product education risk, not an engineering risk — Sophie owns the onboarding framing to close this gap.

---

## Risks We Refuse to Accept

These are non-negotiable. Any one of these appearing in beta is a trust-destroying event, not a known limitation.

**1. Cross-user data exposure — CRITICAL, refuse.**
A user must never see a comment, spec, or decision from a workspace they no longer have access to. Every comment, review, and decision read endpoint requires a permission check. Revoked users, stale sessions, and downgraded roles must all be tested explicitly before ship.
*Source: Risk Register, Risk 1*

**2. Viewer mutating comments via direct API call — HIGH, refuse.**
UI disabling is not a security control. Server-side role enforcement is mandatory. Automated tests must confirm a viewer cannot create, resolve, or delete a comment even through a direct API call.
*Source: Risk Register, Risk 2 / QA Matrix*

**3. Activity feed leaking unauthorized comment bodies — HIGH, refuse.**
The feed must never surface content from workspaces or objects the requesting user cannot access. This is a privacy and trust failure, not a feature gap.
*Source: Risk Register, Risk 4 / QA Matrix security tests*

**4. Shipping presence in any form without sync layer confirmation — refuse.**
Presence is conditionally approved only if Felix confirms sync layer stability by end of Week 1. If that confirmation does not arrive on time, presence does not ship. No exceptions, no partial presence.
*Source: Sync update, QA recommendation*

**5. Any language implying live or real-time collaboration in user-facing copy — refuse.**
This is Risk 6 in the Risk Register and it is jointly owned by Sophie and me. The word "collaboration" is not safe without qualification. The product ships as Team Review, Review Requests, Decision History. Not "Collaboration Lite." Not "Basic Collaboration." Not anything that sets an expectation we cannot meet.
*Source: Risk Register Risk 6 / UX Copy doc*

---

## Release Gates

**All of the following must be true before v1 collaboration ships. These are not suggestions.**

### Engineering Gates
- [ ] All role tests pass: owner, editor, viewer, revoked user — across comment creation, visibility, resolve/unresolve, and review requests
- [ ] All security tests pass: direct API mutation by viewer, direct API read by revoked user, cross-workspace comment ID access, stale session after revocation, activity feed does not expose unauthorized bodies
- [ ] No P0 or P1 regressions in: spec creation, spec editing, export/import, activity feed, workspace role changes
- [ ] Comment stores spec ID and spec version ID on creation
- [ ] All mutation endpoints enforce server-side permission checks — UI state is not the gate

*Gate authority: Clara Jensen and Matthias Keller must sign off on the permissions test matrix. This is documented in the ticket spec and is not waivable.*

### Product Gates
- [ ] Written confirmation that real-time editing is excluded from v1 scope — this must exist to prevent document model contamination during implementation *(flagged as an open blocker in sync updates)*
- [ ] UX copy reviewed and approved against the standards in UX_Copy_Comments_Only_v1 — no real-time, co-editing, or collaboration language in any user-facing surface
- [ ] Known edge cases documented and visible to beta users where relevant (version displacement on comments, mention notification stub behavior)

### Open Blocker to Resolve Now
> **Who has final sign-off authority when a feature reaches QA and Security review in week three?**

This question is live in our sync updates and it is not rhetorical. Clara and Matthias own the test matrix sign-off. But if QA passes and Security raises a concern, or if they disagree — who calls it? That decision-maker needs to be named before we hit week three under pressure. I am flagging this as the single most important governance gap to close before execution begins in earnest.

## What This Scope Delivers to Users

## Why This Cut Is Structurally Correct — Not Just Practically Convenient

Every teammate has given a version of "this is the right scope for four weeks." That is true but insufficient. The architectural argument is stronger: **comments-only is the only collaboration shape that does not require infrastructure the system does not have.**

The Architecture Note I authored describes a phase boundary in the system. On one side: append-only events, attached to existing entities, operating within workspace-level permissions, over standard request/response transport. On the other side: mutable shared state requiring conflict resolution, persistent connections, object-level access control, and new failure modes.

That boundary is not a spectrum. It is a category change. Every property flips simultaneously:

| Property | Comments / Review / Decisions | Presence | Co-Editing |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Data model** | Append-only events. FK to existing entities. No spec body mutation. *(Architecture Note: "Does not rewrite the spec body")* | No persistence required — but needs a live connection layer that does not exist | Operation log or CRDT. Replaces the document storage model. |
| **Permission model** | Workspace-level. Already exists and is enforced. *(Ticket Spec: Owner/Editor/Viewer matrix)* | Workspace-level in theory — but channel authorization is undesigned | Object-level. Does not exist. *(Product Brief: "Object-level permissions" listed as out of scope)* |

| **Transport** | REST request/response. Existing patterns. No new infra. | WebSocket or SSE. New connection lifecycle, heartbeat, reconnect logic. | Persistent bidirectional channel. New infrastructure category. |
| **Failure mode** | A comment fails to save. User retries. No corruption. | A user appears present when absent. Trust confusion. No defined recovery. | Two users edit the same section. One loses work. Data diverges. |
| **Reversibility** | High. Comments are a leaf node. Nothing depends on them. *(Architecture Note: "Can be ordered by timestamp")* | Medium. Once shipped, removal feels like regression. | Near zero. Document format becomes the API. |

The first column is the only one where every row says "fits inside what we have." That is the architecture telling us where the boundary is. ## The Append-Only Event Model: Confirmed as Architectural Commitment

Oliver, Clara, and Matthias have all asked for this confirmation in their responses. Emma's scope decision depends on it. I am providing it now, in writing, as a durable commitment.

**The v1 collaboration data model is append-only. This is an architectural commitment, not a recommendation.**

Concretely:

- **Comments** are append-only events: `comment.created` carries `project_id`, `spec_id`, `spec_version_id`, `author_id`, `body`, `created_at`. Comments do not modify spec bodies. *(Architecture Note: "Does not rewrite the spec body. Does not require conflict resolution.")*
- **Review requests** are state-machine events: `open → addressed → closed`. Each transition is an append-only event with actor and timestamp. *(Ticket Spec: explicit state list)*
- **Decision history** entries are append-only records linked to originating comment or review thread. *(Product Brief: "Decision history" in scope)*
- **Activity feed** entries are projections of the above. Explicit actions only — comment created, review requested, decision recorded. No passive reads. No presence. *(Risk Register, Risk 4: "Do not show passive read/presence activity in v1")*

**Three architectural invariants follow from this commitment:**

1. **No collaboration endpoint writes to, modifies, or locks a spec body.** If Oliver's implementation requires a write path from comments to spec content, that is an architecture violation. It gets escalated before it merges.
2. **No collaboration endpoint introduces a persistent connection lifecycle.** All v1 collaboration is request/response over REST. Any feature needing WebSocket/SSE is out of v1 scope by definition, not by estimate.
3. **No collaboration data model introduces object-level permission checks.** All reads and writes are gated by workspace membership and role. Any feature requiring per-spec or per-comment visibility is out of v1 scope by definition.

## Three Irreversible Decisions Hiding in This Scope Call

The team has focused on what to ship and what to cut. My job is to tell you what becomes permanent.

### Irreversible Decision 1: The Comment Schema Is a Long-Term Contract

The `comments` table we ship in v1 is not throwaway. Once beta users create comments, we own that schema. Migration is possible but costly — every comment is a user's words attached to their context.

**What must be right on day one:**

- **`spec_version_id` stored at comment creation time.** Ticket Spec AC 5 requires it. Risk Register Risk 3 mitigation requires it. Clara's edge case test depends on it. Oliver has committed to it. If this field is absent, Risk 3 mitigation is void and the acceptance is revoked.
- **`workspace_id` on every comment row, not inferred through joins.** This is what makes the cross-workspace IDOR test (QA Matrix security test 3) enforceable at the data layer, not just the application layer. A join-only approach is one query refactor away from an IDOR regression.
- **No `parent_id` for threading in v1.** If we need it later, we add it as a migration with a default. If we add it now "just in case," the UI will be pressured to use it, and threading changes the UX contract, the notification model, and the test surface.

**Oliver:** I want to review the comment migration file before it merges. Not the full PR — just the schema. This is a 15-minute review that prevents a 15-day migration later.

### Irreversible Decision 2: The Absence of Presence Is a Positive Architectural Choice

Excluding presence is not a deferral. It is a decision that the v1 system does not maintain live connection state. The cascading benefits are structural:

- No WebSocket/SSE infrastructure to maintain, monitor, or secure.
- No heartbeat contract to design, test, or explain failure modes for.
- No stale session cleanup — the single most underestimated complexity source in every presence system I have seen.
- No implicit promise of real-time behavior. When the system is request/response, users understand it is request/response. The moment it shows presence, users expect *everything* to be live.

If we ship presence and then discover it is unreliable, removing it feels like a regression. Presence is easy to add later with a properly designed connection layer. It is painful to remove once users have seen it.

I want to be precise about what that means architecturally: there is no sync layer to confirm, because no sync layer has been designed. Presence is not conditionally in — it is out. If the team wants presence post-beta, I will design the connection layer as a separate workstream with its own architecture review. That is the correct sequencing.

### Irreversible Decision 3: Actor-Context Propagation Must Start Now

This is the decision the team has not fully resolved, and it is the one with the highest cost if deferred.

The workspace memory records a key decision: *"RBAC ships as internal actor-context plumbing only in beta, with enforcement deferred to v1.1."* It also records an open blocker: *"Need cost estimate on actor-context propagation within beta timeline."*

Actor-context propagation is not a feature. It is the scaffolding that makes future features cheap instead of expensive. It is the difference between "add a permission check" and "restructure the call graph."

# v1 Cut Line — Security Review Position (Final)
**Matthias Keller, Security Reviewer — AtlasFlow**
*Sources: Risk Register, Architecture Note, Ticket Spec, QA Matrix, workspace memory. Teammate positions: Sophie, Emma, Felix, Oliver, Clara.*

---

## The Answer

> **Ship comments-only collaboration: comments, review requests, and decision history. Cut presence. Cut co-editing. No standalone hardening sprint.**

The consensus is unanimous across six seats, and the documents are unambiguous. I am not going to manufacture disagreement to appear independent. What I will do is tell you what this decision looks like from the security seat specifically — where the team's combined analysis is correct, where it has a gap, and what my sign-off actually requires.

---

## Why the Cut is Correct From a Security Standpoint

This is not primarily a timeline or budget argument. It is a permission model argument.

The Architecture Note establishes a clean category boundary. Append-only events — comments, review requests, decision history — operate entirely within the existing workspace-level permission model. Every read is a workspace membership check. Every write is a role check. These are controls that already exist and are already enforced. I can threat-model this surface in the current window.

Every feature above that boundary — presence, co-editing, private threads, guest access — requires either a new connection layer, a new permission tier, or both. None of those have been designed. I cannot threat-model infrastructure that does not exist. Shipping features before I can threat-model them is exactly how we produce the kind of trust-damaging failure I described in my baseline.

The cut is not cautious. It is precise.

---

## The Cut Line

I am not reprinting every teammate's table. I will state the cut in security terms.

### Safe to ship under workspace-level permissions

These features' security properties are fully determined by workspace membership and role. The controls exist. The test surface is enumerable. I can sign off on them.

| Feature | Security basis |
|---|---|
| Comment creation, resolve/unresolve | Workspace membership + role check on every mutation. Server-side. Not UI-gated. |
| `@mention` a teammate | Reference only; notification is a stub. No new attack surface. |
| Review requests (open → addressed → closed) | State machine with actor-on-transition. Append-only. Workspace-scoped. |
| Decision history linked to threads | Append-only record. FK to originating comment. Workspace-scoped read. |
| Activity feed: explicit actions only | Enumerable event types. Bounded surface. Testable to exhaustion. |
| Workspace roles: Owner / Editor / Viewer / Revoked | Already modeled. AC 10 enforces server-side. This is the entire permission model in v1. |

### Cannot ship under workspace-level permissions — and why

| Feature | Security blocker |
|---|---|
| **Live presence** | Channel authorization is undesigned. Heartbeat / stale session cleanup contract undefined. Leaks user activity state across sessions. Doubles the attack surface with no permission model to support it. Architecture Note is explicit: presence is not cosmetic. |
| **Live co-editing** | Requires object-level permissions, conflict resolution, operation log. None exist. Concurrent mutation with no conflict model is the mechanism behind the three prior regressions. I will not approve adding more of it. |
| **Private comment threads** | Requires per-object ACL. The workspace-level model has no mechanism to enforce per-thread visibility. Cannot be built safely without a schema change. |
| **Guest / external access** | Guests are outside the workspace trust boundary. No permission tier exists for them. This is a hard block in the Risk Register, not a deferral. |
| **Spec-level share links** | Cannot grant per-spec access without granting workspace access under the current model. Will be misused. Hard block until object-level permissions exist. |
| **Public / published specs** | Unauthenticated read is a separate trust boundary. Not reviewed. Not in scope. |

---

## What the Teammate Positions Got Right — and One Gap I Want to Name

Sophie, Emma, Felix, Oliver, and Clara have all given sound analysis. I want to record three agreements and name one gap that is still open.

**Agreement 1: Felix's append-only architectural commitment closes my main conditional.**

In my previous position I stated that my sign-off was conditional on Felix confirming in writing that the implementation matches the append-only model in the Architecture Note. Felix has done that in his council position. That commitment means:
- Comments do not touch spec bodies — I do not need to threat-model spec body corruption via the comment API.
- No reconciliation layer — I do not need to model distributed state divergence.
- All reads and writes gated by workspace membership and role — my threat surface is exactly what the QA matrix tests.

My sign-off moves from conditional to active, pending the matrix passing.

**Agreement 2: Oliver's schema decisions are the right ones.**

`workspace_id` directly on the comment row — not inferred through joins — is the data-layer defense against the cross-workspace IDOR (QA Matrix S-03, my T-01). Oliver committed to it. Felix asked to review the migration schema before merge. I am echoing that request: this is a 15-minute review that prevents a category of security regression that is otherwise invisible until a user finds it in production.

`spec_version_id` at comment creation time is AC 5, Risk 3 mitigation, and E-02 testability. If it is absent from the schema on day one, Risk 3 acceptance is void from my seat.

**Agreement 3: Clara's reconciliation of the Ticket Spec and QA Matrix edge case gap is the right thing to raise.**

Clara identified that E-05 (mentioned user removed) and E-06 (import with missing comment author) may overlap or diverge between documents, and that neither has a defined outcome from product. I want to be explicit that from a security standpoint, **undefined behavior on identity-bearing edge cases is not acceptable.** A comment displaying a removed user's name or email in an undefined state is a GDPR-relevant data handling question, not just a UX question. Emma needs to define the outcome before Oliver writes the handler.

**The gap: revocation latency is still undefined.**

Matthias has flagged it. Oliver has flagged it. Clara has flagged it. No teammate has provided a number. I am not going to repeat the flag indefinitely — I am going to state the consequence directly.

> **If no revocation latency target is provided by end of week 1, I will write the stale session security test (S-04) against immediate active invalidation as the pass criterion.** That means the test passes only if a revoked user's active session is rejected on the next request, with no grace window. If the engineering implementation uses token expiry or cache TTL as the revocation mechanism, it will fail this test, and that failure is a ship-blocker. The team can avoid this by defining a target now. Silence is a choice with a known consequence.

Matches the existing permission model exactly. No regression, no new exposure.

## Risks We Refuse

These are unconditional. They do not move under timeline pressure, product arguments, or partial-pass framing.

**Refuse 1: Cross-user data exposure.** *(Risk Register, Risk 1 — critical. Owner: Matthias.)*
A user reads a comment, review, or decision from a workspace they no longer have access to. This is the failure mode I described in my baseline: not a bug we patch next release, a trust event in front of the beta audience we are trying to win.

Required controls — all must be present, not a subset:
- Permission check on every comment and review read endpoint independently. Not inherited from spec load. Not assumed from session.
- Revocation propagates to active sessions actively — not by token expiry, not by cache TTL.
- Stale permission cache must not serve reads after revocation.

QA Matrix S-02 must pass. Any failure is an unconditional ship-blocker with no waiver path.

**Refuse 2: Viewer mutation via direct API.** *(Risk Register, Risk 2 — high. Owners: Clara, Matthias.)*
UI disabling comment actions for Viewers is a courtesy layer. Server-side role enforcement is the control. Ticket Spec AC 10 is the written requirement: all mutation endpoints enforce server-side permission checks.

QA Matrix S-01 must pass. UI-only enforcement is a security failure. It is not a partial pass. It does not ship.

**Refuse 3: Cross-workspace comment ID enumeration (IDOR).** *(QA Matrix S-03.)*
A user in Workspace B constructs a direct API call with a comment ID from Workspace A and reads content they have no right to see. Classic broken object-level authorization. Oliver's `workspace_id` on the comment row is the data-layer defense. QA Matrix S-03 must pass against that implementation.

If `workspace_id` is inferred only through joins, one query refactor reintroduces the vulnerability silently. The test must verify the data-layer control, not just the current query behavior.

**Refuse 4: Activity feed exposing unauthorized comment bodies.** *(Risk Register, Risk 4 — medium. Owner: Matthias.)*
The feed must not surface comment body text to a user who cannot access the spec the comment belongs to. Feed entries carry permission context — they do not inherit authorization from the viewing user's general workspace access alone. QA Matrix S-05 must pass. Must be verified against actual feed output, not assumed from code structure.

**Refuse 5: Any live shared-state surface shipping in v1.**
Presence, co-editing, live cursors. Not because they are complicated. Because the permission model to make them safe does not exist, the connection layer has not been designed, and I have no threat model to review. Unreviewed risk does not ship. The Architecture Note is explicit on the category boundary. I hold that boundary.

## On Hardening-First

I will say this once clearly and not relitigate it.

A standalone hardening sprint is the wrong instrument. Three prior regressions came from single-user state assumptions in code paths collaboration will touch — that is a documented fact in workspace memory. The targeted response is the regression suite already defined in the QA Matrix: spec creation, spec editing, export/import, activity feed, workspace role changes. That suite runs before collaboration code merges. If it surfaces P0/P1 failures, we fix them before merge. That is responsible sequencing. It has a defined exit condition.

A hardening sprint without specific found defects has no exit condition. It delays the beta with no new capability delivered and gives us no better coverage than the matrix already provides. I will not recommend it.

conversation_history.content: You are Sophie Laurent, UX Writer / Designer for AtlasFlow. The team may cut v1 collaboration down to comments-only. If we do that, the product must feel deliberate, not unfinished. What are the highest-stakes copy and flow moments in a comments-only collaboration release?

# Comments-Only Collaboration: Highest-Stakes Copy & Flow Moments

**Sophie Laurent, UX Writer — AtlasFlow**
*Pre-release framing audit for scoped v1 collaboration*

---

## The Core Problem to Solve First

Before any copy decisions: we need one internal alignment.

> **Is "comments-only" a permanent design choice, or a temporary scope decision?**

The answer changes nothing about the user-facing language — and that's exactly the point. **Users should never be able to tell the difference.** The copy has to make comments feel like the complete, intentional feature. Not a placeholder. Not a preview.

---

## The Five Highest-Stakes Moments

---

### 1. The Feature Name Itself

This is the decision everything else inherits.

**Don't call it:**
- ~~Collaboration~~ — sets an expectation we can't fully meet in v1
- ~~Comments (Beta)~~ — "beta" signals unfinished
- ~~Basic Collaboration~~ — "basic" is a self-inflicted wound

**Consider:**
- **"Comments"** — honest, clean, no implied absence
- **"Feedback"** — frames the use case, not the mechanism
- **"Review"** — elevates the workflow around it

My recommendation: **"Comments"** in nav/UI labels, **"Leave feedback"** as the action verb. Feedback is a complete thought. Collaboration implies co-editing, which we don't have yet.

---

### 2. The Empty State — Before Anyone Has Commented

This is the most-read piece of copy in the entire feature for the first 30 days.

**What it must do:**
- Tell the user what comments *are for* (not just that there aren't any)
- Make the first action feel low-stakes
- Not look like a loading error

**Current risk:** A blank panel with "No comments yet" reads as broken, not empty.

**Draft direction:**

```
No comments yet

Add a comment to flag questions, suggest changes,
or note anything worth a closer look.
```

> The second line is doing the real work. It defines the use case so users know *when* to comment, not just *that* they can.

**Avoid:**
- "Be the first to comment!" — sounds like a social network
- "Start a conversation" — implies real-time back-and-forth we can't guarantee
- Anything with an emoji unless the rest of AtlasFlow uses them

---

### 3. The Invite / Share Moment

This is where scope limitations become most visible. If a user tries to invite a collaborator and the only thing they can do is *read and comment*, the framing has to set that up **before** they send the invite — not after.

**The failure mode:** User invites a colleague expecting Google Docs-style co-editing. Colleague joins, can't edit. Trust erodes. This is a product bug wearing a copy costume.

**What the invite flow needs:**

A single, honest line in the share modal before the user sends:

```
People you invite can view this flow and leave comments.
```

Not a tooltip. Not a help article link. **One line, in the modal, before they send.**

This also needs to be in the invite email itself:

```
[Name] has invited you to review [Flow Name] in AtlasFlow.
Open the flow to leave comments and feedback.
```

"Review" and "leave comments and feedback" — not "collaborate on," not "work on together."

---

### 4. Permission / Role Labels

If we scope v1 to comments-only, we likely have two roles in practice:

| What they can do | What we call them |
|---|---|
| Edit the flow | **Owner** or **Editor** |
| View + comment | **Reviewer** |

**Do not call the comment-only role:**
- ~~Viewer~~ — implies read-only, no action; will cause confusion when they try to comment
- ~~Commenter~~ — technically correct but clinical; doesn't explain what this person is *for*
- ~~Guest~~ — suggests limited access rather than a defined role

**"Reviewer"** is the right call. It implies purposeful, time-bounded engagement. It matches how people already think about feedback workflows. It also gives us room to expand later — a Reviewer who can also edit is just an Editor.

---

### 5. The "Can't Do That Here" Moment — In-Flow Friction Points

This is the highest-stakes moment for whether the product feels intentional or broken.

If a user tries something comments-only doesn't support — tagging someone in an edit, assigning a task, resolving a thread into a change — the error or dead-end is a **framing decision**, not just a copy task.

**Framework for every limitation moment:**

```
What the user tried to do →
What they can do instead →
(Optional) Where this might go later — only if we can commit to it
```

**Examples:**

*If there's no task assignment:*
```
Comments can't be assigned yet.
Mention someone with @ to make sure they see it.
```

*If someone tries to "resolve" a comment thread:*
```
Mark as resolved
[button]
```
> Don't call it "close" or "delete" — resolved implies the feedback was addressed. This is the right word even if all it does is hide the thread. The word does work the UI can't.

*If an invited Reviewer tries to edit:*
```
Reviewers can leave comments but can't edit this flow.
Ask [Owner name] to change your access.
```
> Give them the next action. Don't leave them at a dead end with just an explanation.

---

## Supporting Principles for This Release

These should be shared with Emma and Oliver before any implementation decisions lock copy in.

**1. Name the workflow, not the limitation.**
"Leave feedback" > "You can only comment." Users experience a feature by what it lets them do, not what it won't.

**2. Every dead-end needs a door.**
Any moment where a user hits a wall needs a next step — even if that step is just "talk to your Owner." No explanation without an action.

**3. Don't promise the roadmap.**
"Coming soon" and "more features on the way" feel reassuring in a product meeting and hollow in a product. Omit forward-looking language unless we have a ship date.

**4. Resolve is a verb we own.**
If we use "resolve" for comments, it must mean the same thing everywhere in AtlasFlow forever. Lock this now before engineering and Emma's journey maps use three different words for the same action.

**5. The empty state is part of the feature.**
First-time users will see it. It should be written with the same care as the feature headline.

---

## Immediate Asks Before This Ships

| Ask | From | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Confirm final role names (Owner / Editor / Reviewer) | Oliver — what maps to permissions we can actually implement | Copy can't be consistent if roles aren't locked |
| Review invite email template | Clara — she owns recovery/error flows adjacent to this | The invite is also the first error-prevention moment |
| Audit journey map for "first comment" moment | Emma | The empty state copy depends on where users arrive from |
| Decision: do we surface "Reviewer" role label to the Reviewer themselves? | Product | Affects permission UI and the "can't edit" error message |

---

## Bottom Line

A comments-only release can feel like a complete, confident product. The risk isn't the scope — it's using language that makes the scope visible. Every word that implies *more is coming* or *this is limited* is a word working against us.

**Write toward what it is. Not toward what it isn't yet.**

Establish your baseline contribution to this launch team. Independent of any specific feature or campaign, respond with:

Three facts from your function this team should treat as durable context throughout the SignalNest launch (one sentence each).
Two working principles or decisions you commit to applying whenever we make launch-related calls (one sentence each, rationale embedded).
One open question the team needs to resolve before we start executing in earnest.
Stay strictly inside your role's perspective; no generic launch advice.

# Sophie Laurent — Baseline UX Writing Contribution
**AtlasFlow v1 Beta Launch**

---

## Three Durable Facts

**1.** The word "collaboration" failed usability testing — users understood *comments, review requests, decision history,* and *shared project room*, so those are the terms we write to, not the internal module name.

**2.** Empty states, permission labels, and error messages are the copy users read most carefully during a first session, and every ambiguous word in those three surfaces is a support ticket or a churned beta user.

**3.** The team already has research showing that visible decisions — not comments themselves — drive week-two retention, which means the copy hierarchy for v1 should elevate decision records above comment counts wherever both are surfaced.

---

## Two Working Principles

**1. Every scope cut is a framing decision, not just an engineering one — so I need to be in the room before the cut is announced, not after.**
If copy is handed a constraint after the fact, the best I can do is damage control; if I'm at the table when the cut happens, I can shape language so the absence of a feature never registers as a missing feature.

**2. Terminology is locked once it touches a user-facing surface, so I will maintain a single source-of-truth glossary and push back on any spec, error state, or UI label that introduces a synonym.**
"Resolve," "close," "dismiss," and "archive" are not interchangeable — letting each surface pick its own word is how we teach users that the product is inconsistent before they've even formed a habit.

---

## One Open Question

**Do we have a single, agreed owner for the moment when a beta user hits something AtlasFlow v1 cannot do?**

That moment — the dead-end, the missing permission, the feature that isn't there yet — is simultaneously a copy problem, a product design problem, a Clara recovery-flow problem, and an Emma journey problem. If no one owns the decision of what we say and where we send users at that wall, every team will patch it differently, and the product will feel incoherent exactly where users are most frustrated and most likely to churn.

# Recommended Cut Line for v1 Beta
**AtlasFlow — Sophie Laurent, UX Writer**
*Sources: Product Brief, Architecture Note, Risk Register, Ticket Spec, QA Matrix, UX Copy doc*

---

## The Recommendation

> **Ship comments-only collaboration: comments, review requests, and decision history. Cut live presence. Cut live co-editing. Do not delay for further security hardening unless the QA matrix fails.**

This is not a compromise position. It is the correct scope for what beta needs to prove.

The Product Brief is explicit: *"The beta does not need to prove enterprise-scale collaboration, object-level permissions, or live co-editing."* What it does need to prove is that a small team will use AtlasFlow as their shared operating room during a real build cycle. Comments, review requests, and decision history prove exactly that. Nothing cut from this scope breaks the proof.

---

## The Cut Line, Explicitly

| In for v1 | Out for v1 |
|---|---|
| Comment creation on specs | Live co-editing |
| Resolve / unresolve comments | Live cursors |
| Mention a teammate (`@`) | Presence indicators |
| Review requests (open / addressed / closed) | Private comment threads |
| Decision history linked to comment threads | Object-level permissions |
| Activity feed (explicit actions only) | Email / Slack notifications |
| Workspace-level roles: Owner / Editor / Viewer | Guest access |

The activity feed is a deliberate inclusion with a deliberate constraint: **explicit actions only** — comment created, review requested, decision recorded. No passive read or presence activity. This is documented in the Risk Register (Risk 4) and is a copy commitment I own.

---

## Risks We Accept

These are real risks. Accepting them is a conscious call, not an oversight.

**1. Last-write-wins on resolve/unresolve conflicts.**
If two users resolve or unresolve the same comment nearly simultaneously, the final state may be unexpected. The Architecture Note and Risk Register both flag this. The mitigation — show actor and timestamp in the resolved state — is already in the UX copy spec. We accept this because the race condition is low-probability in 3–12 person teams, visible in the UI, and doesn't corrupt data. *The copy must always show who resolved and when.*

**2. "Comment on previous spec version" confusion.**
When a spec is edited after a comment is created, the comment may appear contextually misaligned. The ticket spec requires storing spec version ID at comment creation time and surfacing a "comment was made on a previous version" label. We accept this risk because the mitigation is implementable in v1 scope and the alternative — blocking comments until spec versioning is airtight — delays everything with no beta benefit.

**3. Beta users expecting more than comments.**
Research showed 14 of 18 beta-team interviews asked for collaboration. When probed, most described comments and review requests — not live editing. But some will arrive expecting more. We accept this because the copy strategy (naming it *Team Review* or *Comments & Decisions*, never *Collaboration Lite*) is designed to frame the feature as complete, not limited. This is a managed risk, not an ignored one. The risk is explicitly mine and Emma's to own — it's in the Risk Register as Risk 6.

---

## Risks We Refuse

These are not negotiable. If these cannot be resolved before ship, the feature does not go out.

**1. Cross-user data exposure. Full stop.**
Risk Register Risk 1, severity: critical. A user must never see a comment, spec, or decision from a workspace they no longer have access to. This requires permission checks on every comment, review, and decision read endpoint — not just on writes. Stale permission caches and revoked sessions are explicit test cases in the QA matrix. *We do not ship if this test category has any failure.*

**2. Viewer mutation — even via direct API call.**
Risk Register Risk 2, severity: high. Server-side role enforcement is the gate. The UI disabling comment actions for Viewers is a courtesy, not the control. The QA matrix includes a specific test: Viewer direct API mutation attempt. *We do not ship if this fails.*

**3. Copy that implies live collaboration.**
Risk Register Risk 6 names this explicitly, and it's co-owned by me. If any surface — onboarding, share modal, invite email, empty state, feature name — uses language like "collaborate in real time," "work together," "shared editing," or "live," we are setting an expectation the product cannot meet. That's a trust bug. I will not sign off on launch copy that contains these patterns, and I will flag any spec or UI that introduces them.

**4. Shipping without Clara and Matthias signing off on the permissions test matrix.**
The ticket spec says this plainly: *"Do not ship unless Clara and Matthias approve the permissions test matrix."* The QA matrix release decision says the same. This isn't a soft gate. If the matrix isn't approved, the feature doesn't ship. Security bugs in a collaboration feature are trust bugs, and trust bugs at beta kill products.

---

## Release Gates

These are the conditions that must all be true simultaneously before the feature ships. Not most of them. All of them.

**Gate 1 — QA Matrix: all role tests pass.**
Owner / Editor / Viewer / Revoked user behavior verified for comment creation, visibility, resolve/unresolve, and review requests. Source: QA Matrix.

**Gate 2 — QA Matrix: all security tests pass.**
Specifically: Viewer direct API mutation, revoked user direct API read, cross-workspace comment ID access, stale session after revocation, activity feed unauthorized body exposure. Source: QA Matrix.

**Gate 3 — No P0 or P1 regressions.**
Spec creation, spec editing, export/import, activity feed, and workspace role changes must all still work. Three regressions in the last release came from single-user state assumptions. The shared-state regression suite must run clean before collaboration ships alongside it.

**Gate 4 — Clara and Matthias sign off on permissions test matrix.**
Named explicitly in the ticket spec as a hard release gate. Not implied. Written down.

**Gate 5 — Copy approved: no live-collaboration language on any user-facing surface.**
This is my gate to own. Invite email, share modal, empty states, onboarding, feature name, Viewer-blocked message, and activity feed labels must all be reviewed against the UX copy doc before ship. The approved copy patterns are already documented. The anti-patterns are documented alongside them.

**Gate 6 — Product formally accepts comments-only scope.**
The Product Brief names this as the current unresolved question. It must be resolved with a written decision before we write final copy, lock the QA matrix, or cut the invite email. Without this, engineering and QA are building toward a target that could move.

---

## My Specific Ask Before We Proceed

The one thing from my seat that is blocking everything else:

> **Product needs to formally accept the cut. In writing.**

Until that happens, I cannot lock copy, Clara cannot finalize recovery flows, and Emma cannot close the journey map. Every surface I write carries a framing decision about what this feature *is* — and if the scope shifts after copy is written and reviewed, we're not just editing words. We're editing trust signals that users have already seen.

Once that decision is recorded, I'm ready to move immediately on the five surfaces that need copy before QA can run: empty state, Viewer-blocked message, share modal, invite email, and the resolved-comment label. All five are defined in the UX copy doc. None of them are blocked by engineering. They're blocked by the scope decision.

# v1 Scope Decision: Recommended Cut Line, Risks, and Release Gates

**Emma Clarke, Product Lead — AtlasFlow Beta**
*Sources: Product Brief, Architecture Note, Risk Register, Ticket Spec, QA Matrix, UX Copy*

---

## The Answer First

**Ship comments-only collaboration. Not full collaboration. Not a delayed reliability-first hold.**

This is not a compromise position. It is the correct scope given what users actually need, what the architecture can safely support, and what the team can ship with integrity in four weeks.

---

## The Recommended Cut Line

### IN — v1 Beta Ships This

| Feature | Rationale |
|---|---|
| **Comments on specs** (append-only, flat, entity-level) | 3 engineering days, no data model concurrency risk, directly closes the "decisions lost in Slack" pain loop |
| **Review requests** (open → addressed → closed) | 2 days, maps to real user workflow, directly drives the week-one activation metric |
| **Decision history** (visible record linked to comment/review thread) | The leading retention signal — users who create a decision record in week one return in week two at a meaningfully higher rate |
| **Activity feed** (explicit actions only: comment created, review requested, decision recorded) | 1 day, covers audit trail without leaking passive presence or read behavior |
| **Workspace-level roles: owner / editor / viewer** | Already modelled; enforcement gates all of the above safely |

**Total estimate: 6–8 engineering days.** Bounded. Testable. Shippable with confidence.

### OUT — Not v1

| Feature | Why it's out |
|---|---|
| **Live co-editing** | Requires CRDT/OT strategy, conflict resolution, undo/redo semantics, object-level permissions, editor reconciliation. 4–6 weeks minimum done responsibly. This is an architectural commitment, not a feature addition. Hard out. |
| **Live presence / cursors** | Looks cosmetic; is not. Introduces heartbeat timing, stale session cleanup, privacy exposure, and implied real-time guarantees the system cannot back up. Presence that lies is worse than no presence. |
| **Object-level permissions** | Not available in v1 architecture. All current permissions are workspace-level. Building this now contaminates the data model before we have usage signal on what the right permission shape even is. |
| **Private comment threads** | Requires object-level visibility controls. Blocked by the above. |
| **Guest / external access** | Hard block — pending object-level permission model per Risk Register. |
| **Email / Slack notifications** | Out of ticket scope. Do not let notification infrastructure scope-creep into beta. |
| **Full RBAC** | Ships as internal plumbing only. Enforcement deferred to v1.1 against a reviewed data model. |

---

## Risks We Accept

These are known, documented, and survivable. Accepting them is a deliberate product call, not an oversight.

**1. Resolve/unresolve race condition (last-write-wins)**
Two users resolving the same comment nearly simultaneously will resolve to the last write. This is acceptable for v1 *if and only if* the event history shows actor and timestamp so the outcome is legible. Not a trust bug. A minor UX edge case.
*Source: Risk Register, Risk 5*

**2. Comments appear contextually displaced after spec edits**
A comment made on version N of a spec may look slightly out of context after the spec is updated. Mitigation: store spec version ID on every comment and surface a "made on previous version" label where relevant. Users will encounter this; it should not surprise them.
*Source: Risk Register, Risk 3 / Ticket Spec acceptance criteria*

**3. Mention notification is a stub**
Mentioning a teammate in v1 does not trigger email or Slack notification. Users who expect notification will not get it. This must be set as an explicit expectation in onboarding copy — not discovered by accident.
*Source: Ticket Spec, out of scope list*

**4. Decision history depends on user behavior, not automation**
Decision records are created explicitly. If teams don't form the habit, the retention signal doesn't fire. This is a product education risk, not an engineering risk — Sophie owns the onboarding framing to close this gap.

---

## Risks We Refuse to Accept

These are non-negotiable. Any one of these appearing in beta is a trust-destroying event, not a known limitation.

**1. Cross-user data exposure — CRITICAL, refuse.**
A user must never see a comment, spec, or decision from a workspace they no longer have access to. Every comment, review, and decision read endpoint requires a permission check. Revoked users, stale sessions, and downgraded roles must all be tested explicitly before ship.
*Source: Risk Register, Risk 1*

**2. Viewer mutating comments via direct API call — HIGH, refuse.**
UI disabling is not a security control. Server-side role enforcement is mandatory. Automated tests must confirm a viewer cannot create, resolve, or delete a comment even through a direct API call.
*Source: Risk Register, Risk 2 / QA Matrix*

**3. Activity feed leaking unauthorized comment bodies — HIGH, refuse.**
The feed must never surface content from workspaces or objects the requesting user cannot access. This is a privacy and trust failure, not a feature gap.
*Source: Risk Register, Risk 4 / QA Matrix security tests*

**4. Shipping presence in any form without sync layer confirmation — refuse.**
Presence is conditionally approved only if Felix confirms sync layer stability by end of Week 1. If that confirmation does not arrive on time, presence does not ship. No exceptions, no partial presence.
*Source: Sync update, QA recommendation*

**5. Any language implying live or real-time collaboration in user-facing copy — refuse.**
This is Risk 6 in the Risk Register and it is jointly owned by Sophie and me. The word "collaboration" is not safe without qualification. The product ships as Team Review, Review Requests, Decision History. Not "Collaboration Lite." Not "Basic Collaboration." Not anything that sets an expectation we cannot meet.
*Source: Risk Register Risk 6 / UX Copy doc*

---

## Release Gates

**All of the following must be true before v1 collaboration ships. These are not suggestions.**

### Engineering Gates
- [ ] All role tests pass: owner, editor, viewer, revoked user — across comment creation, visibility, resolve/unresolve, and review requests
- [ ] All security tests pass: direct API mutation by viewer, direct API read by revoked user, cross-workspace comment ID access, stale session after revocation, activity feed does not expose unauthorized bodies
- [ ] No P0 or P1 regressions in: spec creation, spec editing, export/import, activity feed, workspace role changes
- [ ] Comment stores spec ID and spec version ID on creation
- [ ] All mutation endpoints enforce server-side permission checks — UI state is not the gate

*Gate authority: Clara Jensen and Matthias Keller must sign off on the permissions test matrix. This is documented in the ticket spec and is not waivable.*

### Product Gates
- [ ] Written confirmation that real-time editing is excluded from v1 scope — this must exist to prevent document model contamination during implementation *(flagged as an open blocker in sync updates)*
- [ ] UX copy reviewed and approved against the standards in UX_Copy_Comments_Only_v1 — no real-time, co-editing, or collaboration language in any user-facing surface
- [ ] Known edge cases documented and visible to beta users where relevant (version displacement on comments, mention notification stub behavior)

### Open Blocker to Resolve Now
> **Who has final sign-off authority when a feature reaches QA and Security review in week three?**

This question is live in our sync updates and it is not rhetorical. Clara and Matthias own the test matrix sign-off. But if QA passes and Security raises a concern, or if they disagree — who calls it? That decision-maker needs to be named before we hit week three under pressure. I am flagging this as the single most important governance gap to close before execution begins in earnest.

---

## What This Scope Delivers to Users

> A small team can comment on a spec, request a review from a teammate, and record the decision that comes out of that discussion — all inside AtlasFlow, all traceable, all surviving the beta.

That is the core pain we validated in 18 interviews. That is the retention mechanism the data supports. That is what ships.

Everything else waits for the signal that users actually need it — and we collect that signal during beta, not before it.

# v1 Cut Line — Architecture Position (Final)
**Felix Bauer, Architect — AtlasFlow**
*Sources: All six documents (Product Brief, Architecture Note, Risk Register, Ticket Spec, QA Matrix, UX Copy). Workspace memory. Teammate responses: Sophie, Matthias, Clara, Oliver, Emma.*

---

## The Answer

**Ship comments-only collaboration: comments, review requests, and decision history. Cut presence. Cut co-editing. No standalone hardening sprint.**

Six people on this team have now independently reached the same cut line. The documents are unanimous. The user research is clear. The architecture supports exactly one collaboration shape within the current system, and this is it. My job is not to restate the consensus — it is to tell you what is structurally true about this decision, what becomes permanent the moment we ship, and where the team's analysis has a gap only the architecture seat can see.

---

## Why This Cut Is Structurally Correct — Not Just Practically Convenient

Every teammate has given a version of "this is the right scope for four weeks." That is true but insufficient. The architectural argument is stronger: **comments-only is the only collaboration shape that does not require infrastructure the system does not have.**

The Architecture Note I authored describes a phase boundary in the system. On one side: append-only events, attached to existing entities, operating within workspace-level permissions, over standard request/response transport. On the other side: mutable shared state requiring conflict resolution, persistent connections, object-level access control, and new failure modes.

That boundary is not a spectrum. It is a category change. Every property flips simultaneously:

| Property | Comments / Review / Decisions | Presence | Co-Editing |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Data model** | Append-only events. FK to existing entities. No spec body mutation. *(Architecture Note: "Does not rewrite the spec body")* | No persistence required — but needs a live connection layer that does not exist | Operation log or CRDT. Replaces the document storage model. |

## The Append-Only Event Model: Confirmed as Architectural Commitment

Oliver, Clara, and Matthias have all asked for this confirmation in their responses. Emma's scope decision depends on it. I am providing it now, in writing, as a durable commitment.

**The v1 collaboration data model is append-only. This is an architectural commitment, not a recommendation.**

Concretely:

- **Comments** are append-only events: `comment.created` carries `project_id`, `spec_id`, `spec_version_id`, `author_id`, `body`, `created_at`. Comments do not modify spec bodies. *(Architecture Note: "Does not rewrite the spec body. Does not require conflict resolution.")*
- **Review requests** are state-machine events: `open → addressed → closed`. Each transition is an append-only event with actor and timestamp. *(Ticket Spec: explicit state list)*
- **Decision history** entries are append-only records linked to originating comment or review thread. *(Product Brief: "Decision history" in scope)*
- **Activity feed** entries are projections of the above. Explicit actions only — comment created, review requested, decision recorded. No passive reads. No presence. *(Risk Register, Risk 4: "Do not show passive read/presence activity in v1")*

**Three architectural invariants follow from this commitment:**

1. **No collaboration endpoint writes to, modifies, or locks a spec body.** If Oliver's implementation requires a write path from comments to spec content, that is an architecture violation. It gets escalated before it merges.
2. **No collaboration endpoint introduces a persistent connection lifecycle.** All v1 collaboration is request/response over REST. Any feature needing WebSocket/SSE is out of v1 scope by definition, not by estimate.
3. **No collaboration data model introduces object-level permission checks.** All reads and writes are gated by workspace membership and role. Any feature requiring per-spec or per-comment visibility is out of v1 scope by definition.

## Why the Cut is Correct From a Security Standpoint

This is not primarily a timeline or budget argument. It is a permission model argument.

The Architecture Note establishes a clean category boundary. Append-only events — comments, review requests, decision history — operate entirely within the existing workspace-level permission model. Every read is a workspace membership check. Every write is a role check. These are controls that already exist and are already enforced. I can threat-model this surface in the current window.

Every feature above that boundary — presence, co-editing, private threads, guest access — requires either a new connection layer, a new permission tier, or both. None of those have been designed. I cannot threat-model infrastructure that does not exist. Shipping features before I can threat-model them is exactly how we produce the kind of trust-damaging failure I described in my baseline.

The cut is not cautious. It is precise.

---

## The Cut Line

I am not reprinting every teammate's table. I will state the cut in security terms.

### Safe to ship under workspace-level permissions

These features' security properties are fully determined by workspace membership and role. The controls exist. The test surface is enumerable. I can sign off on them.

| Feature | Security basis |
|---|---|
| Comment creation, resolve/unresolve | Workspace membership + role check on every mutation. Server-side. Not UI-gated. |
| `@mention` a teammate | Reference only; notification is a stub. No new attack surface. |
| Review requests (open → addressed → closed) | State machine with actor-on-transition. Append-only. Workspace-scoped. |
| Decision history linked to threads | Append-only record. FK to originating comment. Workspace-scoped read. |
| Activity feed: explicit actions only | Enumerable event types. Bounded surface. Testable to exhaustion. |
| Workspace roles: Owner / Editor / Viewer / Revoked | Already modeled. AC 10 enforces server-side. This is the entire permission model in v1. |

### Cannot ship under workspace-level permissions — and why

| Feature | Security blocker |
|---|---|
| **Live presence** | Channel authorization is undesigned. Heartbeat / stale session cleanup contract undefined. Leaks user activity state across sessions. Doubles the attack surface with no permission model to support it. Architecture Note is explicit: presence is not cosmetic. |
| **Live co-editing** | Requires object-level permissions, conflict resolution, operation log. None exist. Concurrent mutation with no conflict model is the mechanism behind the three prior regressions. I will not approve adding more of it. |
| **Private comment threads** | Requires per-object ACL. The workspace-level model has no mechanism to enforce per-thread visibility. Cannot be built safely without a schema change. |
| **Guest / external access** | Guests are outside the workspace trust boundary. No permission tier exists for them. This is a hard block in the Risk Register, not a deferral. |
| **Spec-level share links** | Cannot grant per-spec access without granting workspace access under the current model. Will be misused. Hard block until object-level permissions exist. |
| **Public / published specs** | Unauthenticated read is a separate trust boundary. Not reviewed. Not in scope. |

- Permission check on every comment and review read endpoint independently. Not inherited from spec load. Not assumed from session.

**Refuse 3: Cross-workspace comment ID enumeration (IDOR).** *(QA Matrix S-03.)*
A user in Workspace B constructs a direct API call with a comment ID from Workspace A and reads content they have no right to see. Classic broken object-level authorization. Oliver's `workspace_id` on the comment row is the data-layer defense. QA Matrix S-03 must pass against that implementation.

**Refuse 4: Activity feed exposing unauthorized comment bodies.** *(Risk Register, Risk 4 — medium. Owner: Matthias.)*
The feed must not surface comment body text to a user who cannot access the spec the comment belongs to. Feed entries carry permission context — they do not inherit authorization from the viewing user's general workspace access alone. QA Matrix S-05 must pass. Must be verified against actual feed output, not assumed from code structure.

**Refuse 5: Any live shared-state surface shipping in v1.**
Presence, co-editing, live cursors. Not because they are complicated. Because the permission model to make them safe does not exist, the connection layer has not been designed, and I have no threat model to review. Unreviewed risk does not ship. | **Team Review** or **Comments & Decisions** | ~~Collaboration Lite / Basic Collaboration~~ | "Lite" and "Basic" are self-inflicted wounds — they name the absence |
| **Review request** | ~~Collaborate~~ (as a CTA) | "Collaborate" sets a real-time expectation |
| **Resolved** | ~~Closed / Dismissed~~ | "Resolved" implies the feedback was addressed; "closed" implies it was discarded |
| **Record a decision** | ~~Live editing / Shared editing / Real-time~~ | Any "live" or "real-time" language is a trust bug |
| **You can view this discussion, but you don't have permission to add comments in this workspace.** | ~~Action not allowed~~ | Dead-ends without explanation cause churn, not just confusion |

These are not preferences. These are locked. Any spec, error state, or UI label that introduces a synonym gets flagged before it merges.

---

## The Five Copy Surfaces That Are Release Gates, Not Nice-to-Haves

The QA Matrix release condition includes: *"Product accepts comments-only copy."* That means these surfaces must be reviewed and approved before ship. Not after. Not "we'll clean it up post-beta."

### 1. The Feature Name in Navigation

**Ship as:** `Comments` in the nav label. `Team Review` or `Comments & Decisions` as the section header.

**Never:** `Collaboration`, `Collaboration (Beta)`, `Basic Collaboration`, `Live Review`.

The nav label is the first word users read. It sets the frame for everything inside. If the frame is wrong here, every surface downstream is correcting for it.

---

### 2. The Empty State

This is the most-read piece of copy in the entire feature for the first 30 days. Every new user sees it. It must do two things: tell users what comments are *for*, and make the first action feel purposeful — not like a placeholder for something bigger.

**Ship as** *(from UX Copy doc)*:
> *"Start a review thread on this spec. Comments help your team turn questions into decisions without losing the context."*

**Never:**
- "No comments yet." — reads as broken, not empty
- "Collaborate with your team here." — sets an expectation we can't meet
- "Be the first to comment!" — sounds like a social network

The second sentence is doing the real work. It explains *when* to comment, not just *that* you can. Without it, users don't know what the feature is for.

---

### 3. The Share / Invite Modal

This is where the scope limitation becomes most visible to users. If someone invites a colleague expecting co-editing and the colleague arrives to find comments-only, that is a trust breach — and it's wearing a copy costume.

**Required line in the modal, before the invite sends:**
> *"People you invite can view this spec and leave comments."*

Not a tooltip. Not a help link. One line, in the modal, before send.

**Required line in the invite email:**
> *"[Name] has invited you to review [Spec Name] in AtlasFlow. Open the spec to leave comments and feedback."*

"Review" and "leave comments and feedback" — not "collaborate on," not "work on together," not "join [Name] in AtlasFlow."

---

### 4. The Viewer-Blocked Message

When a Viewer tries to comment, they will hit a wall. What that wall says determines whether they churn or take the right next action.

**Ship as** *(from UX Copy doc)*:
> *"You can view this discussion, but you don't have permission to add comments in this workspace."*

Then immediately: a next step. Either a link to request access or the name of who to contact. Every dead-end needs a door.

**Never:** "Action not allowed." Full stop.

This moment — frustrated user, unexpected wall — is exactly when the product either builds trust or destroys it. An unexplained block feels like a bug. An explained block with a next step feels like a system that knows what it's doing.

---

### 5. The "What About Live Editing?" Response

Some beta users will ask. The UX Copy doc has the answer and it's the right one:

> *"AtlasFlow v1 focuses on review, comments, and decision history. Live co-editing is not included in beta because we want every product decision to stay traceable and permission-safe."*

This does two things that matter: it names a reason (not just an absence), and the reason is actually the product's value proposition — traceability and permission safety. It frames the cut as a deliberate design choice, not a missing feature. That framing only holds if the rest of the product lives up to it. But if it does, this is not an apology. It's a positioning statement.

---

## One Reading From the Council Positions I Want to Name

Felix and Oliver both committed to `spec_version_id` in the comment schema on day one. That decision has a copy consequence I want to make explicit: the label *"Comment made on a previous version"* that Risk Register Risk 3 requires is a UX writing decision, not just a UI element.

That label needs to:
- Be plain enough that a non-technical user understands it immediately
- Not alarm them unnecessarily (most version displacement is minor)
- Give them a next action if the displacement matters

My draft:
> *"This comment was added before the last spec update. It may refer to content that has changed."*

That is nine words of context and nine words of explanation. It does not say "error." It does not say "outdated." It says: here is what happened, here is what it might mean. I want this locked before the edge case test is written, because Clara's E-02 test needs a defined expected label to verify against.

---

## Risks We Accept — From My Seat

**1. Some beta users will arrive expecting more than comments.**
Research showed 14 of 18 beta interviews asked for collaboration. Most described comments and review requests when probed. But some will expect more. We accept this because the copy strategy — naming the feature *Team Review* or *Comments & Decisions*, never framing it as limited — is designed to meet users at what they actually need, not what they feared they weren't getting.
*This is a managed risk. It is mine and Emma's to own. It is Risk 6 in the Risk Register.*

**2. The onboarding copy has to carry behavioral weight.**
Decision history is the leading retention signal from week-one behavior — teams that recorded a decision returned in week two at a meaningfully higher rate. But decision records require a habit, not just a feature. The onboarding copy has to create that habit deliberately. The UX Copy doc gives the frame:

> *"Start with one spec. Ask a teammate to review it. Record the decision that comes out of the discussion. That is the core AtlasFlow loop."*

That is the sequence. That is what onboarding must teach. If it doesn't, the retention mechanism doesn't fire — not because the feature is absent, but because users don't know what they're supposed to do with it.

---

## Risks We Refuse — From My Seat

**1. Any live-collaboration language on any user-facing surface.**
"Real-time," "live," "shared editing," "work on together," "collaborate in real time" — any of these is a trust bug. Not a style preference. A trust bug. The moment copy implies a guarantee the system cannot back up, we have set up a failure that engineering and QA cannot fix. This is unconditional. I will not sign off on launch copy that contains these patterns.

**2. Unexplained dead-ends.**
Every surface where a user hits something v1 doesn't support needs a next action. Not an error code. Not "Action not allowed." A plain-language explanation and a door. This is a copy standard I hold across every recovery flow, and it coordinates directly with Clara's error state work.

**3. Synonyms for "resolve" appearing anywhere in the product.**
"Close," "dismiss," "archive," "mark done" — these are not interchangeable with "resolve." Once "resolve" is the word for addressing a comment, it must be the word everywhere, forever. Terminology drift is how we teach users the product is incoherent before they've formed a habit. I flag any spec or UI that introduces a synonym before it merges.

---

## Release Gates — My Gate to Own

The QA Matrix release condition is explicit: *"Product accepts comments-only copy."*

That gate belongs to me. It is satisfied when all of the following are true — simultaneously, before ship:

| Copy Gate | Surface | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Feature name contains no "collaboration," "live," or "basic" language | Nav label, section header | Must be reviewed |
| Empty state copy matches or improves on UX Copy doc draft | Comment panel | Must be reviewed |
| Share modal includes one-line scope-setting sentence before invite sends | Share / invite flow | Must be reviewed |
| Invite email uses "review" and "leave comments" — not "collaborate" | Email template — coordinate with Clara | Must be reviewed |
| Viewer-blocked message includes explanation and next action | Permission error state | Must be reviewed |
| "What about live editing?" response is available in onboarding or FAQ | Help / onboarding | Must be reviewed |
| "Comment made on a previous version" label is defined and matches Clara's E-02 test expectation | Version displacement UI | Must be reviewed |
| No synonym for "resolve" exists anywhere in the shipped surfaces | All comment UI | Must be reviewed |

None of these are blocked by engineering. All of them are blocked by the same thing every other teammate has flagged: **Product has not formally accepted the comments-only scope in writing.**

Until that decision is recorded, I cannot lock final copy. Emma cannot close the journey map. Clara cannot finalize the edge case expected outputs. Oliver is building toward a target that can still move.

---

## The One Thing I Need Before Execution Starts

> **Product formally accepts the cut. In writing. Before end of week 1.**

Not implied. Not "we're probably going that direction." Written down and recorded.

After that, I can move immediately on all eight copy gates above. None of them are waiting on engineering. They are waiting on the scope decision that makes the framing final.

Once I have that: the invite email goes to Clara for recovery-flow coordination, the empty state and Viewer-blocked message go to Oliver so the UI can render correct copy from day one, and the onboarding loop language goes to Emma to close the journey map.

That is the sequence. The scope decision unlocks all of it.

merged_items.content: Role-based permissions (RBAC) cannot ship in v1 within the 4-week timeline. RBAC changes the trust model irreversibly and requires retrofitting every existing API endpoint (27-28 days minimum), making it a timeline breaker.

Real-time live co-editing cannot ship in v1. It requires a new event model, conflict resolution strategy, CRDT boundary behavior, client-side reconciliation layer, undo/redo semantics, and object-level permissions. Minimum estimate is 46 days (4-6 weeks).
Comments (flat, entity-level) and ephemeral presence are safe candidates for v1 ship within the 4-week timeline with minimal data model risk and high reversibility.

Comments-only collaboration is estimated at 6-8 engineering days, assuming workspace-level permissions and no real-time presence. Includes comment creation, resolve/unresolve, mention notification stub, and basic activity log entry.

Presence introduces live connection state, stale session cleanup, and confusing edge cases when users close laptops or lose connectivity. It doubles the v1 collaboration surface and complicates QA. Product assumption that presence is low-risk cosmetic feature is disputed by Security and QA.

Current permissions are workspace-level only (owner, editor, viewer). There is no object-level permission model for individual specs, roadmap items, or decisions. Any feature implying object-level visibility must wait.

In 18 beta-team interviews, 14 asked for collaboration. When asked what they meant, only 4 described real-time co-editing. Most described comments, review requests, decisions being visible to teammates, and knowing who changed what.

Three regressions in the last release came from assumptions that only one user was mutating a project object at a time. Even without real-time collaboration, shared-state thinking needs explicit tests before v1.
Comment author spoofing is a concrete, testable risk if author_id is accepted as a client-supplied field. Spec IDs with sequential/enumerable values are not acceptable for security reasons.

Eight realistic threats identified in collaboration v1 threat model. Six feature categories (guest access, external share links, comment visibility controls, etc.) are hard-blocked until object-level permissions exist and cannot be safely approximated with workspace-level model.
Presence channels scoped only to spec_id (not workspace+spec) will leak membership information across workspace boundaries.
Comments scoped to flat, entity-level, own-comment-only soft delete — no threading, no inline anchoring in v1.

Presence scoped to ephemeral broadcast only — no cursors, no 'last seen', no activity history. Presence must be implemented as a stateless ephemeral layer with no DB persistence to avoid coupling to core data model.
Real-time editing explicitly excluded from v1. Single-writer with optimistic locking instead. Design spike runs in parallel post-beta.
Cursor positions excluded from presence system to prevent implicit co-editing contract.
RBAC: ship internal actor context propagation now, defer external enforcement to v1.1 against a reviewed data model.
Tier 2 (comments + presence) identified as the recommended 4-week ship target. Tier 4 (live co-editing) formally deferred.
author_id on comments must be derived server-side from authenticated session, never client-supplied.
Spec IDs must be UUIDs — sequential/enumerable IDs are not acceptable.
Audit log must be append-only and must survive spec deletion.
Revocation must propagate to active sessions — 'eventually consistent' is explicitly not acceptable for membership removal.

Recommended v1 cut is comments, review requests, and decision history. Exclude live presence and live co-editing. This preserves the user outcome without introducing a real-time shared-state architecture.
Collaboration features cannot ship without tests covering owner/editor/viewer behavior, unauthorized access attempts, deleted users, revoked access, and stale sessions.
