Filename: Product_Brief_AtlasFlow_v1_Beta.md  
Pinned to: Emma Clarke, Felix Bauer, Sophie Laurent

Content:
AtlasFlow is a collaborative product-planning workspace for small technical teams. It keeps specs, architecture decisions, QA risks, and launch-readiness work connected.

Beta goal:
The v1 beta should prove that small product teams will use AtlasFlow as their shared product operating room during a real build cycle. The beta does not need to prove enterprise-scale collaboration, object-level permissions, or live co-editing.

Primary user:
Founder-led product teams with 3–12 people building a v1 product, internal tool, or major feature release.

Primary users usually have:
- scattered specs
- Slack decisions
- architecture notes
- QA checklists
- unclear scope cuts
- no durable decision history

Core user pain:
Teams do not lose work because they lack tools. They lose work because product decisions, implementation constraints, security concerns, and QA risks live in different places.

Repeated user language:
- “We decided this somewhere, but I can't find why.”
- “The spec says one thing, engineering built another.”
- “QA finds the edge cases too late.”
- “Security review happens after the feature is already basically done.”

v1 in scope:
- Shared project room
- Product specs
- Comments on specs
- Review requests
- Decision history
- Basic activity feed
- Workspace-level roles: owner, editor, viewer
- Launch checklist
- QA risk tags

v1 out of scope:
- Live co-editing
- Live cursors
- Object-level permissions
- Private comment threads
- External guest access
- Enterprise audit export
- Custom roles
- Advanced workflow automation

Success metrics:
Activation:
- User creates or imports one spec.
- User creates one review request.
- User records one decision.

Retention:
- Team returns within 7 days.
- At least two teammates comment or review.

Quality:
- No cross-user permission leaks.
- No unresolved P0/P1 collaboration bugs.
- Comments and decision history survive export/import.

Current unresolved scope question:
Should v1 ship comments-only collaboration, comments plus presence, full collaboration, or no collaboration until permissions and sync are hardened?

Current evidence favors comments + review requests + decision history, but Product has not yet accepted the cut.

Filename: Architecture_Note_Shared_State_and_Collaboration_Boundaries.md  
Pinned to: Felix Bauer, Oliver Brooks, Matthias Keller

Content:
Collaboration is not a single feature. It is a stack of increasingly complex shared-state promises.

Safe v1 path:
- comments
- review requests
- decision history
- activity feed

Risky live shared-state path:
- presence
- live cursors
- co-editing
- object-level visibility

Current architecture:
AtlasFlow currently stores project objects as versioned records:
- specs
- architecture notes
- risks
- decisions
- checklist items

Writes are sequential. Most screens assume one user is editing a given object at a time. This is acceptable for single-user or asynchronous team review. It is not sufficient for live co-editing.

Safe v1 model:
Comments and review requests can be modeled as append-only events attached to a spec or decision.

Example event:
comment.created with project_id, object_id, author_id, body, and created_at.

Why this is safe:
- Does not rewrite the spec body.
- Does not require conflict resolution.
- Can be ordered by timestamp.
- Can be tested with normal request/response flows.
- Works with workspace-level permissions.

Risky model: live presence.
Presence looks simple but creates hidden promises:
- user activity status
- heartbeat timing
- stale session cleanup
- privacy expectation
- connectivity edge cases
- perceived real-time guarantee

Presence is not only cosmetic. If AtlasFlow shows a user as present when they are not, or absent when they are reviewing, it creates confusion. If activity state is exposed in the wrong workspace, it creates a trust issue.

Not v1: live co-editing.
Live co-editing requires:
- operation log or CRDT/OT strategy
- conflict resolution
- undo/redo semantics
- offline behavior
- editor reconciliation
- object-level permissions
- broader regression matrix

Recommendation:
Ship append-only collaboration:
- comments
- review requests
- decision history
- activity feed

Do not ship:
- live cursors
- live co-editing
- private threads
- object-level restricted comments

Preferred feature names:
- Team Review
- Review Requests
- Decision History

Avoid:
- Collaboration Lite
- Real-time collaboration
- Shared editing

Filename: Risk_Register_Permissions_Sync_Collaboration.md  
Pinned to: Matthias Keller, Clara Jensen, Felix Bauer

Content:
Risk 1: Cross-user data exposure.
Severity: critical.
Owner: Matthias.
Description: A user sees a comment, spec, or decision from a workspace they no longer have access to.
Cause: stale permission cache, missing workspace access check, revoked user session not respected.
Required mitigation:
- Permission check on every comment/review/decision read.
- Tests for revoked users.
- Tests for viewer/editor/owner access.
- No object-level private content in v1.

Risk 2: Viewer can mutate comments.
Severity: high.
Owner: Clara and Matthias.
Description: A viewer can create, resolve, or delete comments despite read-only role.
Required mitigation:
- Server-side role check.
- UI disables actions, but server remains source of truth.
- Automated tests for viewer attempting mutation.

Risk 3: Comment attached to wrong spec version.
Severity: medium-high.
Owner: Clara.
Description: User comments on a spec, but later edits make the comment appear attached to the wrong context.
Required mitigation:
- Store target object id and version id.
- Show “comment was made on previous version” where needed.
- Regression test on spec update after comment.

Risk 4: Activity feed leaks user behavior.
Severity: medium.
Owner: Matthias.
Description: Activity feed reveals that a user viewed or edited something when they expected not to expose activity.
Required mitigation:
- v1 activity feed shows explicit actions only: comment created, review requested, decision recorded.
- Do not show passive read/presence activity in v1.

Risk 5: Resolve/unresolve race.
Severity: medium.
Owner: Clara and Oliver.
Description: Two users resolve/unresolve the same comment close together; final state is confusing or wrong.
Required mitigation:
- Last-write-wins acceptable for v1 if event history is visible.
- Test concurrent resolve/unresolve requests.
- Show actor and timestamp.

Risk 6: Product overpromises collaboration.
Severity: high.
Owner: Sophie and Emma.
Description: Product copy implies live collaboration while v1 only supports comments/review.
Required mitigation:
- Avoid real-time and co-editing language.
- Use review together and record decisions.
- Explain v1 scope clearly in onboarding.

Filename: Ticket_Spec_Comments_Only_Collaboration.md  
Pinned to: Emma Clarke, Oliver Brooks, Clara Jensen

Content:
User story:
As a project teammate, I want to comment on a spec and request review, so that product and engineering decisions can be discussed and recorded without leaving AtlasFlow.

Scope:
Build comments and review requests on specs.

In scope:
- Add comment to a spec.
- View comment thread on a spec.
- Resolve and unresolve a comment.
- Mention a teammate by name.
- Create review request assigned to teammate.
- Close review request.
- Show decision link when a comment results in a recorded decision.
- Activity feed entry for comment created, comment resolved, review requested, review closed.

Out of scope:
- Live co-editing.
- Live cursors.
- Presence indicators.
- Private comments.
- Object-level permissions.
- Guest comments.
- Email notifications.
- Slack notifications.

Permissions:
Owner:
- create, edit own comment, resolve/unresolve, delete own comment, create review request

Editor:
- create comment, edit own comment, resolve/unresolve, create review request

Viewer:
- view comments only
- cannot create, edit, resolve, or request review

Revoked user:
- cannot read or mutate comments

Acceptance criteria:
1. Editor can create a comment on a spec.
2. Editor can resolve and unresolve a comment.
3. Viewer can see comments but cannot create comments.
4. Revoked user cannot read comments.
5. Comment stores spec id and spec version id.
6. Comment thread displays actor and timestamp.
7. Review request can be assigned to an existing teammate.
8. Closing a review request creates an activity feed entry.
9. Comment actions appear in activity feed.
10. All mutation endpoints enforce server-side permission checks.
11. Existing single-user spec editing still works.
12. Export/import preserves comments and review requests.

Edge cases:
- User is removed from workspace while comment form is open.
- Spec is edited after comment is created.
- Two users resolve the same comment at nearly the same time.
- Mentioned teammate is archived or removed.
- Viewer attempts mutation through direct API call.
- Import bundle contains comments from missing users.

Estimate:
- Core comments: 3 engineering days.
- Review requests: 2 engineering days.
- Activity feed integration: 1 engineering day.
- Tests and regression: 2 engineering days.
- Total: 6–8 engineering days.

Release gate:
Do not ship unless Clara and Matthias approve the permissions test matrix.

Filename: QA_Matrix_Collaboration_RC.md  
Pinned to: Clara Jensen, Oliver Brooks, Matthias Keller

Content:
Goal:
Verify comments-only collaboration is safe enough for v1 beta.

Roles to test:
- Owner
- Editor
- Viewer
- Revoked user

Core tests:
Comment creation:
- Owner can create.
- Editor can create.
- Viewer is blocked.
- Revoked user is blocked.

Comment visibility:
- Owner can view.
- Editor can view.
- Viewer can view.
- Revoked user is blocked.

Resolve/unresolve:
- Owner can resolve/unresolve.
- Editor can resolve/unresolve.
- Viewer is blocked.
- Revoked user is blocked.

Review request:
- Owner can create/close.
- Editor can create/close.
- Viewer is blocked.
- Revoked user is blocked.

Regression tests:
- Existing spec creation still works.
- Existing spec editing still works.
- Existing export/import still works.
- Existing activity feed still works.
- Existing workspace role changes still work.

Edge-case tests:
- Remove user while comment form is open.
- Downgrade editor to viewer while form is open.
- Resolve comment from two browser sessions.
- Edit spec after comment created.
- Import bundle with comment author missing.
- Delete spec with comments.
- Restore archived spec with comments.

Security tests:
- Viewer direct API mutation attempt.
- Revoked user direct API read attempt.
- Cross-workspace comment id access attempt.
- Stale session after access revoked.
- Activity feed does not expose unauthorized comment bodies.

Release decision:
Ship only if all role tests pass, all security tests pass, no P0/P1 regressions exist, known issues are documented, and Product accepts comments-only copy.

Filename: UX_Copy_Comments_Only_v1.md  
Pinned to: Sophie Laurent, Emma Clarke, Clara Jensen

Content:
Naming principle:
Do not call this Collaboration Lite.

The v1 feature is not a smaller version of live collaboration. It is a focused review workflow.

Preferred names:
- Team Review
- Review Requests
- Comments & Decisions
- Decision Review

Avoid:
- Collaboration Lite
- Limited collaboration
- Basic collaboration
- Real-time collaboration
- Live editing

Empty state:
Better:
“Start a review thread on this spec. Comments help your team turn questions into decisions without losing the context.”

Avoid:
“Collaborate with your team here.”

Add comment placeholder:
Better:
“Ask a question, flag a risk, or suggest a decision...”

Avoid:
“Write a comment...”

Review request CTA:
Better:
“Request review”

Avoid:
“Collaborate”

Viewer blocked message:
Better:
“You can view this discussion, but you do not have permission to add comments in this workspace.”

Avoid:
“Action not allowed.”

Resolved comment copy:
Better:
“Resolved by Emma Clarke · linked to decision DEC-014”

Avoid:
“Closed”

Feature limitation note:
If users ask about live editing:
“AtlasFlow v1 focuses on review, comments, and decision history. Live co-editing is not included in beta because we want every product decision to stay traceable and permission-safe.”

Onboarding note:
“Start with one spec. Ask a teammate to review it. Record the decision that comes out of the discussion. That is the core AtlasFlow loop.”

items.title: 14 of 18 beta teams asked for collaboration, but only 4 described real-time co-editing.
items.content: In 18 beta-team interviews, 14 asked for collaboration. When asked what they meant, only 4 described real-time co-editing. Most described comments, review requests, decisions being visible to teammates, and knowing who changed what.

items.title: Current shared-state model supports comments but not concurrent document editing.
items.content: The current data model can support append-only comments and review events with moderate risk. It does not support concurrent editing safely without introducing a new event model, conflict resolution strategy, and client-side reconciliation layer.

items.title: Comments-only collaboration is estimated at 6–8 engineering days.
items.content: Comments-only collaboration is estimated at 6–8 engineering days, assuming workspace-level permissions and no real-time presence. Includes comment creation, resolve/unresolve, mention notification stub, and basic activity log entry.

items.title: Comments plus presence is estimated at 12–16 engineering days.
items.content: Presence introduces live connection state, stale session cleanup, and confusing edge cases when users close laptops or lose connectivity. It doubles the v1 collaboration surface and complicates QA.

items.title: Full live co-editing is estimated at 4–6 weeks and should not be in v1.
items.content: Full live co-editing requires a new event model, conflict resolution, editor-state reconciliation, undo/redo semantics, and object-level permissions. Estimate is 4–6 weeks if done responsibly.

items.title: Role-based permissions are currently workspace-level, not object-level.
items.content: Current permissions are workspace-level: owner, editor, viewer. There is no object-level permission model for individual specs, roadmap items, or decisions. Any feature that implies object-level visibility must wait.

items.title: Last release had 3 regressions caused by shared-state assumptions.
items.content: Three regressions in the last release came from assumptions that only one user was mutating a project object at a time. Even without real-time collaboration, shared-state thinking needs explicit tests before v1.

items.title: Highest-retention beta users created at least one decision record in their first week.
items.content: Teams that created a decision record in week one were much more likely to return in week two. Comments may be valuable primarily because they lead to visible decisions, not because comments themselves are the core value.

items.title: Users dislike collaboration module as a label.
items.content: In usability walkthroughs, collaboration module sounded internal. Users understood comments, review requests, decision history, and shared project room.

items.title: v1 beta launch date is fixed; scope is variable.
items.content: v1 beta launches in 4 weeks. The date is fixed because of customer commitments and investor demo timing. Scope is variable. If a feature cannot meet test/security gates, it gets cut or narrowed.

items.title: No full live co-editing in v1 unless evidence changes materially.
items.content: Full live co-editing is not v1. The engineering and QA cost is disproportionate to the evidence. If users continue asking for real-time editing after comments/review ship, revisit post-beta with a separate event-model design.

items.title: Boring tools default remains active.
items.content: Prefer boring, proven tools. Any new framework or collaboration library requires written justification: problem solved, alternatives, integration cost, security review, and exit strategy.

items.title: Every collaboration feature requires explicit permissions tests.
items.content: Collaboration features cannot ship without tests covering owner/editor/viewer behavior, unauthorized access attempts, deleted users, revoked access, and stale sessions. A collaboration bug is a trust bug.

items.title: v1 collaboration copy must frame comments-only as deliberate.
items.content: If v1 ships comments-only, the product copy should frame it as review and decision flow, not limited collaboration. The absence of live editing should not be presented as a missing feature.

items.title: v1 should ship comments + review requests + decision history, not live presence.
items.content: Recommended v1 cut is comments, review requests, and decision history. Exclude live presence and live co-editing. This preserves the user outcome — team review and visible decisions — without introducing a real-time shared-state architecture. Needs final signoff from QA and Security.

metadata.template_source: Emma Clarke, Felix Bauer, and Oliver Brooks

items.title: Presence indicators are low risk.
items.content: Product assumption was that presence indicators are low risk because they are only cosmetic. Security and QA dispute this. Presence exposes user activity state, creates stale-session edge cases, and may imply real-time guarantees the system does not actually provide.

items.title: Add third-party real-time collaboration framework for v1.
items.content: Rejected because integration cost, data-model mismatch, and security review exceeded the v1 window. Felix flagged exit-strategy risk. Matthias flagged supply-chain and permission-model uncertainty. Oliver concluded the framework solves live co-editing, which is not required for v1.

items.title: Original v1 scope included live presence.
items.content: Original v1 collaboration scope included comments, review requests, live presence, and decision history. Superseded after implementation estimates and QA/security review showed presence doubled complexity without clearly improving first-week activation.

items.title: v1 beta
items.content: The first external beta release of AtlasFlow, scheduled for 4 weeks from today. Scope can be cut; date is fixed.

items.title: comments-only collaboration
items.content: Users with workspace access can comment on specs, resolve/unresolve comments, mention teammates, and create review requests. No live co-editing, no live cursors, no object-level private threads.

items.title: review request
items.content: A lightweight workflow where one teammate asks another to review a spec, decision, or roadmap item. Review request status can be open, addressed, or closed.

items.title: decision history
items.content: A visible record of product/architecture decisions linked to the relevant spec, comment, or review thread. This is the core value of v1 collaboration.

items.title: object-level permissions
items.content: Permission checks on individual specs, roadmap items, comments, or decisions. Not available in v1. Current permissions are workspace-level.

items.title: shared state
items.content: Any product state that more than one user can read or mutate. Shared state requires explicit tests for ordering, stale data, permissions, and conflict handling.
Collaboration requests from 14 of 18 beta interviews resolve to async review and decision visibility — not live co-editing — which means the conservative v1 scope is user-aligned, not a compromise
Decision visibility (not comments) is the leading retention signal from week-one user behavior, which should reorder how we sequence and message collaboration features
Collaboration is not one feature but four (comments, presence, RBAC, real-time editing) with radically different architectural footprints and reversibility profiles
Current data model supports append-only operations safely but has no conflict resolution for concurrent mutations — confirmed by three regressions in the last release
Permission model is workspace-level only; any feature implying object-level visibility is blocked until a new permission layer is designed
A prior Yjs-based collaboration framework was already evaluated and rejected, establishing precedent for the infrastructure review gate
Tier 3 role-based permissions requires retrofitting every existing API endpoint, not just adding new ones — this is the primary reason it breaks the 4-week window
Workspace-level permissions are the only enforced permission model in the current codebase — any promise of object-level or per-spec access control is currently unenforceable
Full live co-editing is a 10-week minimum project based on CRDT/OT requirements — it should not appear in any v1 commitment
Full live collaboration is not a 4-week shippable scope from a testability standpoint — this is now a documented position, not an open debate
Absence of object-level permissions is a hard constraint on any v1 feature implying restricted or private access, regardless of UI completeness
Offline and interrupted-session behavior has no defined contract and no named owner, making those surfaces formally untestable right now
Workspace-level permissions are confirmed as the v1 boundary — object-level ACLs are explicitly deferred, and this constraint must be treated as documented scope, not final design
Three prior regressions from single-user mutation assumptions elevate concurrent-state threats from theoretical to demonstrated risk, which changes prioritization of T-05 and T-04 mitigations

Several collaboration features assumed to be v1 candidates (guest access, spec share links, public specs, comment visibility controls) are reclassified as hard blocks pending object-level permission model
The word 'collaboration' is not safe to use in user-facing copy — validated terms are comments, review requests, decision history, and shared project room
Decision records drive week-two retention more than comment counts, which changes copy hierarchy priorities for v1 surfaces
The comments-only scope cut is a framing decision with copy implications, not just an engineering constraint — this reframes when UX Writing needs to be in scope discussions
Live co-editing is deferred from v1 on both build-cost and trust-risk grounds
